issues.body: _name_bindings walks every assignment in every scope, and _module_launcher_aliases resolves them as one file-global, monotonic fixpoint. Consequently an unrelated local assignment such as `def helper(): runner = subprocess.run` can cause a module-level `def f(run=runner)` to be reported even when the module-level `runner` is a safe helper. Likewise, a launcher assignment after a default taints the earlier default although Python evaluates that default before the later assignment. The transitive_backwards known-positive enshrines this error: at module execution its `def go(..., runner=_ALIAS)` raises NameError, so it never captures a launcher. This is the scope/order defect called out in round 1, now converted into intentional over-collection rather than resolved.
issues.fix_hint: Resolve each default against bindings visible in its actual lexical scope at the point the default is evaluated. Respect statement order and shadowing/rebinding, while retaining AnnAssign and transitive Name support. Replace the reverse-order positive with executable fixtures, and add independent negatives proving that later assignments, function-local assignments, and same-named bindings in unrelated scopes do not create findings.
issues.title: Alias resolution still ignores scope and binding order

verdict.summary:
> 🤖 SPARQ agent

The round adds independent positives for annotated and transitive aliases, but the prior major is not fully resolved. The resolver deliberately discards Python scope and execution-order semantics: assignments anywhere in the AST permanently taint an identifier everywhere, including assignments after a default or inside an unrelated function. That makes the enrolled standing gate reject safe defaults based on bindings that cannot supply their values. The reverse-order fixture pins this unsound behavior using a function definition that would itself fail with NameError when executed, so it does not validate the claimed import-time capture hazard. A trust-plane gate must be conservative without manufacturing evidence; this remains a major correctness defect.
